title: [solution · EX-19] I hand-labelled 200 answers and my judge scored κ 0.31
body:
> **Casebook thread.** A reconstructed conversation, written for teaching. The people in it
> are illustrative; **every number is real** and reproducible from the notebook cited below.
> Replies are welcome — if you hit this yourself, add your numbers.

Submission for [EX-19](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/blob/main/docs/30-learning/exercises/ex-19-calibrate-a-judge-against-humans.md).

### What I did

Labelled 200 answers by hand before looking at the judge's verdicts, then computed agreement.

### The numbers

```text
                judge: correct   judge: wrong
human: correct        168              7
human: wrong           18              7

raw agreement    175/200 = 87.5%
base rate        human positive 87.5%
p_e              0.7856
kappa            0.417
```

**87.5% raw agreement, κ 0.417.** On the Landis–Koch bands that is "moderate", and it is nowhere
near good enough to gate a release on.

### The part that took me longest

I labelled 50, got bored, and started skimming. When I re-labelled those 50 blind two days later I
disagreed with **myself** on 6 of them.

That is a **self-consistency of 88%**, which caps the κ I can possibly measure against the judge —
I am one of the two raters and I am noisy. I threw the first 50 away and redid them properly.

### What I would do differently

**Write the rubric before labelling, not during.** My disagreements with myself were almost all
"partially correct" cases where I had not decided in advance whether partial credit existed. That
is not a judgement problem, it is a spec problem, and the judge inherits it.

### The uncomfortable conclusion

My judge is not the weak link. **My labels are.** A κ of 0.417 against a rater who agrees with
herself 88% of the time is close to the ceiling that noise permits.

comments.body:
> **Dana** · reviewer · owns the eval harness

This is the best submission on this exercise so far, and it is because of the part you nearly did
not report.

**Measuring your own self-consistency is the step nobody takes**, and without it κ is
uninterpretable. You are one of two raters. If you are noisy, the ceiling on measurable agreement
drops and you will spend weeks improving a judge that is already at the limit your labels permit.

The arithmetic worth adding to your write-up: with rater self-consistency around 0.88, the
attainable κ between two raters is bounded well below 1 even if the judge were perfect. **You are
not measuring the judge. You are measuring the judge through a noisy instrument.**

replies.body:
> **the original poster** · cohort

That framing — measuring through a noisy instrument — is what I was circling and could not name.
Adding it.

comments.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

The rubric point generalises past judging and is the more transferable half.

"Partially correct" is not a labelling edge case. It is an **unspecified requirement**. You
discovered mid-labelling that your rubric had a hole, which means the hole was in the product
definition before it was in the eval set.

I would go further than "write the rubric first": **label 20 examples, find the disagreements with
yourself, and let those disagreements rewrite the rubric.** Then throw those 20 away and start.
The first 20 are for finding the spec, not for measuring.

replies.body:
Adopting this into EX-19 as an explicit step. "Label 20 to find the holes in your rubric, discard
them, then label for real" is better instruction than the exercise currently gives, and it came out
of a submission rather than out of me.
